There are educators who teach concepts. Then there are people who quietly alter your life trajectory without even realising they did.

Dr Aman Bhonsle has been that person for me.

I first learned under him 7 years ago through Transactional Analysis at a point where I was trying to figure out where life was taking me professionally and personally. Confused. Curious. Slightly chaotic. Trying to make sense of myself and the world.

Then came Aman.
AND WHAT AN EXPERIENCE.

I genuinely don't think I have laughed till I cried in classrooms the way I have learning under him.

The man is a RIOT.

Psychologically brilliant. Ridiculously well-read. Sharp. Hilarious. Deeply human. Pop-culturally dangerous in the best way possible because somehow he'll explain a concept using something absurdly relevant and suddenly your brain decides to store it forever.

His examples live in my head RENT FREE years later.
And you don't even realise you're learning because you're too busy laughing.

Then halfway through the lecture he casually says one line that sends you into a full blown existential crisis. And that's his superpower, because you leave feeling lighter, smarter, stronger and more aware.
Like life is manageable and not so hard to face again.
Fast forward 7 years.
I'm almost 30 now. Married. A psychotherapist myself. Still learning. Still terrified by certain life chapters. Still trying to become a better human.

And somehow Aman enters this chapter too through Parenting Coaching.
Now see, some people give information.
Some people give perspective.
Very few give people confidence in themselves.
But he does so effortlessly.
But what stays with me isn't just what he teaches.
It's who he is.
The consistency. The care. The investment. The meticulously detailed material, the depth of dedication. The remembering people years later. The rooting for people. The wanting people to do well in life.
I've done enough trainings and courses over the years to know this isn't common.
People remember what you teach, sure, maybe.
People never forget how you made them feel.
Years later, I still remember both.
That says everything.
Aman you, my friend are a ROCKSTAR!

He offers premium therapy services for individuals, couples, families, and groups who want to work through depression, anxiety, trauma, OCD, loneliness, anger, guilt, relationship difficulties, and feelings of worthlessness, hopelessness, and helplessness. owner_posts.post_text:
Self-Esteem and Identity Therapy

Low self-esteem can affect far more than confidence. It can shape your decisions, relationships, ambitions, self-expression, and the way you speak to yourself every day. You may struggle with self-doubt, shame, insecurity, harsh self-criticism, body image concerns, or a deeper confusion about who you are and what you really want. In therapy, I do not offer surface-level confidence advice. I help you understand how these patterns developed, why they keep repeating, and what may be needed for real change. My style is reflective, depth-oriented, and emotionally engaged. Therapy can help you build a more stable sense of self, reduce self-attack, trust your own mind more, make clearer decisions, and begin living with greater confidence, authenticity, and self-respect.

Trauma Therapy

Trauma can continue affecting you long after the painful event is over. It may show up as fear, emotional overwhelm, numbness, mistrust, shame, panic, relationship difficulties, or feeling that the past is still shaping how you respond in the present. Sometimes people do not even think of their experience as trauma, but they know something in them still feels unsettled, guarded, or deeply hurt. In therapy, I work in a paced, respectful, and emotionally containing way. My approach is depth-oriented and sensitive to both emotional safety and the deeper impact of painful experiences. The aim is not to force you to relive what happened, but to help you process it, understand its effects, reduce its hold on your life, and gradually build a stronger sense of safety, stability, and emotional freedom.

Overthinking and OCD Therapy

Overthinking and OCD can leave you feeling trapped inside your own mind. You may keep replaying things, doubting yourself, checking, analysing, seeking reassurance, or struggling with intrusive thoughts that feel upsetting, confusing, or hard to control. These patterns can take away peace of mind, drain energy, and make even simple decisions feel exhausting. In therapy, I work with both the distress you are facing and the deeper emotional patterns that may be keeping these cycles active. My style is careful, non-judgmental, and psychologically in-depth, while still practical enough to help you respond differently in daily life. Therapy can help you reduce the grip of obsessive thinking, feel less controlled by fear and doubt, and regain a greater sense of freedom, clarity, and trust in yourself.

Depression Therapy

Depression is not always obvious from the outside. Sometimes it looks like low mood, tiredness, emptiness, irritability, loss of interest, emotional numbness, crying spells, or simply feeling stuck in survival mode. It can affect motivation, sleep, work, relationships, and your sense of meaning in life. In therapy, I offer a space where your suffering is taken seriously and explored with care. My approach is thoughtful, emotionally attentive, and depth-oriented, with focus on both what is happening now and what may be shaping it underneath. Therapy can help you understand what is weighing you down, reduce self-criticism, reconnect with yourself, and slowly begin to feel more alive, more hopeful, and more able to engage with life again in a meaningful way.

Anxiety Therapy

Anxiety can make daily life feel heavy, tense, and difficult to switch off from. You may find yourself constantly worrying, overthinking, feeling restless, panicky, physically on edge, or expecting something to go wrong even when things seem fine on the surface. Over time, anxiety can affect sleep, work, relationships, confidence, and your ability to feel settled in yourself. In therapy, I help you understand not only the symptoms, but also the emotional patterns and pressures that may be driving them. My style is calm, thoughtful, and depth-oriented, while still practical and grounded. The aim is not just temporary relief, but a deeper sense of steadiness, better emotional regulation, clearer thinking, and the ability to face life with more confidence and less fear.

Anger and Emotional Regulation Therapy

Anger often carries more beneath it than people realise. It may involve frustration, hurt, resentment, helplessness, shame, or feeling repeatedly misunderstood and overwhelmed. When anger shows up as irritability, harsh tone, emotional outbursts, jealousy, impulsive reactions, or difficulty calming down, it can damage relationships, create tension at work or home, and leave you feeling guilty afterward. In therapy, I help you understand not just the anger itself, but what happens inside you before it escalates. My style is direct, thoughtful, and emotionally focused, without being shaming or moralistic. Therapy can help you become less reactive, regulate emotions better, communicate more clearly, and respond with more control, maturity, and steadiness in difficult situations.

Some messages stay with you. 🌿

A young student I supported during her board exam phase recently wrote to share that she scored 98 and felt that our work together helped her stay calmer, steadier, and able to function well under pressure.

Moments like these are deeply meaningful. Academic performance is never only about intelligence or effort; emotional containment, clarity, and psychological support can make a real difference when it matters most.

Grateful to be trusted in such important phases of people’s lives.

featured_reviews.review_text:
I started therapy with Dr. Tejas Shah during the COVID period in 2020, when I was in a very difficult mental state. Living near Worli sea face, constantly hearing ambulance sirens, reading about COVID, and knowing that older people and those with heart problems were more vulnerable made me extremely anxious. I stopped going out, lost 12 kg, stopped working, and gradually slipped into mild depression. Even basic daily routines became difficult.

Although I was advised to take antidepressants, I was not in favor of psychotropic medication. On the recommendation of my psychologist, I began talk therapy with Dr. Tejas Shah—initially twice a week, and later up to five times a week.

Over time, therapy helped me not only with the fear and distress of that period, but also with long-standing issues of self-doubt, self-criticism, lack of confidence, and feeling “not good enough.” Since 2024, I have gradually reduced therapy to twice a week, which I continue till now (April 2026).

Today, I feel much more relaxed, less self-critical, and more socially at ease. I enjoy conversations, feel more spontaneous, and am much less shy than before. I also see the difference in my professional work. I am calmer with patients, more attentive, and more confident in explaining medical as well as psychological aspects of their condition. I feel I am maturing into a better Psycho-Dermatologist.

At the age of 80, I continue to work, pursue my PhD, journal daily, and stay mentally active. I still have some challenges, such as anxiety before presentations, but I can clearly see how much progress I have made.

I find Dr. Tejas Shah to be a very good analyst—patient, attentive, and a deeply thoughtful listener. His integrative therapy approach has helped bring about meaningful change in my life. I intend to continue therapy with him, now twice a week, for as long as my mind permits.

owner_posts.post_text: Phone addiction has become one of the biggest parenting challenges today. Parents struggle with setting boundaries, managing constant conflicts, monitoring online safety and competing with the appeal of screens. Many also feel guilty because they use phones themselves. The goal is not to eliminate technology, but to teach children balance, responsibility and healthy digital habits.

Growing up, many of us were taught that parents are the safest people to talk to. But sometimes children don’t need advice, solutions, or life lessons — they just need to feel heard. When emotions are dismissed often enough, silence slowly starts feeling safer than honesty. And what looks like distance is sometimes just someone protecting parts of themselves that once felt misunderstood.

Sometimes I wonder how a person can be considered “too young” to fully understand consequences, yet old enough to commit something so horrific. It’s difficult to balance accountability with the belief that people can change.

We often underestimate how stressed corporate professionals can be. Long hours, constant deadlines, endless notifications, pressure to always perform, and the inability to truly switch off slowly take a toll. Just because someone is sitting in an office, dressed well, and functioning normally does not mean they are mentally okay. Think about it.
Yet another time with one of my favourites,

Working with Godrej has always been a fun-filled experience—each time they come up with something unique that has a psychological tinge to it. This time, we explored how safe spaces actually change our perceptions and perspectives. 

Hyderabad was fun.
Another city coming soon.

Children today are growing up inside powerful digital systems that shape attention, self-worth and emotional safety. Instead of reacting with outrage or blanket bans, the conversation must centre on protection. Thoughtful guardrails and digital literacy can help young people build resilience before stepping into a world designed to capture them.

I am often asked, “In a room full of testosterone, does your cortisol soar?”
Well, no but my dopamine certainly does. And toward the end, my serotonin spikes too. The only one periodically off the charts is insulin -  but yes, oxytocin will always be my favourite.

Why emotionally unavailable relationships keep repeating — and how your patterns shape them.

Most people believe they keep attracting emotionally unavailable partners.
But what I often see in therapy is this, people stay in emotionally unavailable relationships longer than they should.

Not because they don’t know better.
But because something in the pattern feels familiar.

We start:
• Explaining behaviour
• Waiting for clarity
• Overgiving to feel chosen

And slowly, the dynamic gets shaped.
Emotional availability isn’t just about who you meet.

It’s also about what you tolerate, how you respond, and what you choose to stay in.

You've had the conversation. More than once.
And yet you're back at the same place.

It's not that you're not trying. It's that most couples are stuck in a pattern they can't see and no amount of talking fixes what you haven't named yet.

In couples work, I've seen five patterns come up again and again. Each one looks like a communication problem on the surface. Underneath, something else entirely is going on.

Feeling like you’re the only one trying in a relationship is not just painful. It is exhausting.

Usually, it starts with good intentions.
And slowly, the relationship becomes uneven.

Not always because the other person does not care.
But because a pattern gets created where one person over-functions and the other under-functions.

That is why trying harder does not always make things better.
Sometimes, it only keeps the same dynamic going.

Not all relationship issues come from lack of effort.

Sometimes, they come from a difference in how both partners relate to change.

One partner naturally leans toward growth:
They notice patterns
They bring up conversations
They want things to improve

The other leans toward acceptance:
They feel things are fine
They don’t see the same urgency
They prefer things to stay easy

And this creates a repeating tension:
One feels, “We need to work on this”
The other feels, “Why are we creating problems?”

Over time:
• Growth starts feeling like criticism
• Acceptance starts feeling like avoidance

And both partners feel misunderstood.

This is often called the change partner vs acceptance partner dynamic.

It’s not about who is right.
It’s about understanding what each person is trying to protect.

The Mental Load Nobody Talks About in Romantic Relationships

Who remembers the birthdays, plans the weekends, checks in after difficult days, and keeps the relationship running?

The mental load isn't always visible—but it can quietly shape how connected partners feel. When one person carries most of the planning, remembering, and emotional responsibility, resentment can build even in loving relationships.

At The Intimacy Curator, we help individuals and couples explore communication, shared responsibility, and emotional awareness—because feeling supported isn't just about what gets done, but how it's shared.

Sometimes the strongest relationships aren't the ones doing more—they're the ones carrying it together.

Build more conscious, balanced relationships with The Intimacy Curator.

"Nothing's wrong."

Sometimes those words mean exactly that. But sometimes they signal that conversations have become too difficult, needs have gone unspoken, or partners have stopped expecting to be understood.

Healthy relationships aren't defined by the absence of conflict—they're strengthened by the ability to talk about what matters.

At The Intimacy Curator, we help individuals and couples create space for honest conversations, emotional awareness, and deeper connection.

Sometimes the most important relationship question isn't "Are we fighting?" It's "Are we still talking?"

 Discover more intentional ways to reconnect with The Intimacy Curator.

Reconnect beyond burnout with The Intimacy Curator

From boardrooms to deadlines, many successful professionals spend their days performing at a high level. But when stress becomes constant, emotional energy can become depleted — leaving little room for connection at home.

For many couples in fast-paced cities like Mumbai, Delhi, and Bangalore, what feels like a loss of intimacy is often the result of burnout, mental overload, and emotional exhaustion.

When you're constantly in "doing" mode, it becomes harder to be present, vulnerable, and connected with your partner.

At The Intimacy Curator, we support individuals and couples in understanding the impact of stress on relationships, improving communication, and creating space for meaningful connection. Because intimacy isn't just about time together — it's about emotional availability.

In fast-paced cities like Bangalore, many couples spend their days managing work, responsibilities, and constant mental overload — leaving little room for emotional connection.

Over time, even caring relationships can begin to feel distant, routine, or emotionally disconnected.

Working with an intimacy coach is not about “fixing” your relationship overnight. It’s about understanding communication patterns, emotional needs, stress responses, and creating healthier ways to reconnect.

At The Intimacy Curator, we offer a supportive space for individuals and couples to explore intimacy, emotional closeness, and relationship dynamics with greater awareness and compassion.

If you’ve been feeling emotionally distant despite sharing the same space, small intentional changes can make a meaningful difference.

Why Rest Matters for Healthy Relationships Too

When people are exhausted, connection becomes harder.

Patience gets shorter. Communication feels heavier. Even affection can begin to feel like effort instead of comfort.

Rest is not only personal care — it also affects how we show up emotionally in relationships.

At The Intimacy Curator, we explore how stress, overwhelm, and emotional fatigue influence intimacy, and how couples can create more balance and connection in everyday life.

Feeling Emotionally Close Again After Months of Distance

Emotional distance rarely happens overnight.

It often grows slowly through busy schedules, routine conversations, exhaustion, and the absence of meaningful connection.

The good news is that intimacy can be rebuilt through small, intentional moments of presence, curiosity, and emotional openness.

At The Intimacy Curator, we help couples reconnect gently — without pressure, blame, or unrealistic expectations.

Why Some Conversations Turn Into Arguments So Quickly

Sometimes, the issue isn’t the topic — it’s the emotional buildup underneath it.

Many couples find themselves reacting strongly to small moments because stress, unmet needs, or feeling unheard has been accumulating quietly over time.

Learning how to pause, listen, and respond differently can change the emotional tone of a relationship more than “winning” an argument ever will.

At The Intimacy Curator, we support individuals and couples in creating healthier emotional communication patterns with more awareness and less defensiveness.

The Hidden Impact of Constant Busyness on Emotional Connection

Modern life rarely slows down.

Between work, responsibilities, and constant notifications, many couples spend time together — but not truly with each other.

Busyness doesn’t just take away time.
It takes away presence.

Small moments of connection — a conversation, a shared pause, a simple check-in — often get replaced by distraction and fatigue.

Over time, this can create a subtle but growing disconnect.

Rebuilding intimacy doesn’t always require big changes.
Sometimes, it starts with small, intentional moments of attention.

At The Intimacy Curator, we help individuals and couples become more present in their relationships — so connection feels natural again, not forced.

Because intimacy lives in the moments we don’t rush through.

When You Feel Lonely in a Relationship That Looks “Perfect”

From the outside, everything may seem fine.

You spend time together.
There’s stability.
Maybe even shared goals and routines.

And yet, inside, there’s a quiet sense of loneliness.

This experience is more common than we admit.
Because emotional connection isn’t measured by appearances — it’s felt in how seen, heard, and understood you are.

Sometimes, couples don’t need to fix everything.
They just need to rediscover how to truly connect beyond the surface.

At The Intimacy Curator, we support couples in moving from functional relationships to meaningful ones — where both partners feel emotionally met.

You’re allowed to want more than “everything looks okay.”

Relearning Touch: Why Physical Closeness Feels Uncomfortable for Some Adults

For some, physical closeness doesn’t always feel natural or easy — and that’s rarely talked about.

Discomfort with touch can come from past experiences, stress, or simply not feeling fully present in your body.

It’s not about something being “wrong.”
It’s often about your system needing more safety, awareness, and time.

Relearning touch isn’t about pressure or performance.
It’s about reconnecting — slowly, gently, and with consent — to what feels comfortable and real for you.

At The Intimacy Curator, we create a space where individuals and couples can explore connection at their own pace, without judgment.

Because true intimacy begins where comfort and safety meet.
